title: India-Raised Harvard Student Co-Creates $300 Concussion Headset, Wins Global Dyson Prize
headline: India-Raised Harvard Student Co-Creates $300 Concussion Headset, Wins Global Dyson Prize
subheadline: Rumble Rims, built by Radhika Saran, Cleo Pontone and Sophia DeVito, uses infrared eye-tracking to give coaches an objective sideline read on possible concussion — and beat a record 2,294 entries to the $40,000 award.
summary: Rumble Rims, built by Radhika Saran, Cleo Pontone and Sophia DeVito, uses infrared eye-tracking to give coaches an objective sideline read on possible concussion — and beat a record 2,294 entries to the $40,000 award.

body:
• Rumble Rims, a sideline concussion-screening headset built by Harvard students Cleo Pontone, Radhika Saran and Sophia DeVito, has won the Global Medical category of the 2026 James Dyson Award.
  • Saran grew up in Bengaluru and Mumbai and trained as an architect before joining Harvard's Master's in Design Engineering programme.
  • The 3D-printed headset costs about $300 to make, runs a two- to three-minute infrared eye-tracking test, and comes with a $40,000 prize to fund the next prototype.
  • It is a screening tool, not a diagnosis: return-to-play decisions stay with a qualified healthcare professional.

A low-cost headset that screens athletes for possible concussion on the sideline has won the Global Medical category of the 2026 James Dyson Award. Rumble Rims was created by three second-year students in Harvard University's Master's in Design Engineering programme — Cleo Pontone, Radhika Saran and Sophia DeVito — and was selected by Sir James Dyson from a record 2,294 entries across 28 countries and regions — the highest number in the competition's history, according to the award.

The team will receive $40,000 — about Rs 37 lakh — to accelerate development, according to the award announcement. Rumble Rims first won the US James Dyson Award and advanced to the Global Top 20 in October before taking the medical category.

The India-raised co-inventor

Saran grew up in India, in Bengaluru and Mumbai, and is an alumna of Delhi Public School who trained as an architect before moving into design engineering at Harvard. She has been clear about the device's limits. "It in no way is a diagnosis at this point," she told Yahoo News.

How the headset works

Concussion is difficult to spot in the moment: symptoms differ from person to person and can take up to 72 hours to appear, while objective assessment tools are often expensive, clinic-based or dependent on specialists. That leaves schools and youth leagues relying on subjective sideline judgement. Rumble Rims is built for exactly that gap: during a two- to three-minute test, side-mounted infrared cameras and 45-degree dichroic mirrors measure how an athlete's eyes follow, fixate and move — behaviour that can indicate possible neurological impairment. A mobile display turns the measurements into real-time guidance on whether the athlete should come off and be referred for professional assessment.

The 3D-printed headset costs about $300 to produce. A recovery dashboard supports repeat testing over time, giving athletes, families and clinicians an objective record to track progress before a return to play. The team reached the design after prototyping helmets, mouthguards and chin rests, with feedback from medical professionals and coaches.

"Cleo, Radhika and Sophia have found a new way to bring objective screening to the sidelines, where the critical decisions are made. It could help prevent the lasting brain injuries that affect so many sportsmen and women."

— Sir James Dyson

What the prize money does next

The team plans to build a higher-fidelity prototype, refine the eye-movement assessment and validate the headset with athletes, coaches, trainers and medical advisers. The longer-term aim is pilots with schools and youth sports programmes and, eventually, medical device validation. "The recognition from the James Dyson Award validates our belief that we don't have to accept problems as they stand today," the three inventors said in a joint statement.

The James Dyson Award, now in its 21st year, has supported more than 400 student inventions since 2005. For parents of young athletes, Rumble Rims is not yet something to buy or ask a school for — it is a prototype entering testing. What changes now is the funding and scrutiny behind it: if validation holds up, an objective sideline check that today needs a clinic could become a $300 piece of kit in a coach's bag.
